catalog_quote: This is likely why Nurse (2000) notes that there are the 7 as well as 5 vowel transcriptions in previous documentation. Vowel length is not contrastive. [p. 411] ... Some sounds appear mixed possibly due to the influence of the Swahili alphabet as speakers insisted on how some sounds should be written even though Swahili and Dhaisu have significant differences. ... Nurse (2000) also notes such mixtures. Some of the vowel features may be influenced by tones, which have not been marked in this study. [p. 412] ... Future research calls for an exploration of tone and its possible role in the merger and other processes. [p. 424]

new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule for stress is given anywhere. The only accessible phonological description treats Dhaisu as having tones (left unmarked in the data) and non-contrastive vowel length; word stress/accent is not mentioned at all.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source does not discuss stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Elicited citation-form words (six speakers from Bwiti, recorded in Dar es Salaam 2017 and Tanga 2018); the tone remark is an aside about transcription, not a description of the prosodic system. Treat as 'tonal, stress undescribed', not as a stress statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Dhaiso = Dhaisu = Daiso/Daisũ = Kidaiso/Kidhaiso (dhai1238, dhs, Guthrie E56). Speakers and outsiders often call it 'Segeju' (they self-identify as 'highland Segeju'), but the coastal Segeju language (ISO seg) is a different, Digo-based variety; Nurse 1982 and Ngonyani et al. 2022 keep the two apart. The 2022 data come from speakers from Bwiti (East Usambara, Tanga Region), recorded 2017-2018; the 2019 book is in Swahili.

sources.citation: Anonymous reviewer. 2020. Review of Josephat Rugemalira, Ann Biersteker, Deo Ngonyani & Angelina Nduku Kioko, Kidaiso: Sarufi na msamiati (Nairobi: Twaweza Communications, 2019, viii+224 pp., ISBN 978-9966-028-95-2). Tanzanian Affairs 126 (May 2020), Reviews.
sources.note: Review only: reports that part 1 of the book 'outlines the sound system and grammar' and that older speakers use seven vowels, younger ones five; vocabulary Daiso-Swahili-English pp. 49-148, English-Daiso pp. 149-223. The review says nothing about tone or stress.
No linguistic content; cites Maho & Sands 2002 (The languages of Tanzania: a bibliography), Nurse 1982 and Nurse 2000 as the literature on the language.

sources.note: The fullest English description of Daiso (phonology, nominal and verbal morphology, lexicon, compared with Kamba); the 2022 chapter relies on it for the vowel system and notes it discusses transcription mixtures. The single most likely place for an explicit statement on tone/stress in Daiso.
